# Draft:The Weekly Register (18th-century periodical)

The Weekly Register was a London‑based opposition weekly published from 1732 to 1735.
Edited chiefly by political writer James Ralph, the paper attacked the administration of Robert Walpole, championing the Patriot‑Whig agenda.
History
The first issue appeared on 7 January 1732, priced at two‑pence and printed “for J. Peele at the Lock’s‑Head in Pater‑noster‑Row.”
Each issue filled a folio half‑sheet in double columns, opening with a leading essay and followed by parliamentary summaries and foreign news digests.
Ralph supplied most of the leading pieces—often signed “Regulus” or “Amicus Candidus”—denouncing Walpole’s fiscal and colonial policies.
Circulation reached “upwards of 3,000” by mid‑1733, placing the paper among the larger Patriot weeklies of the decade.
On 14 March 1733 the House of Commons ordered the printer into custody for a breach‑of‑privilege article; publication was suspended for three weeks and resumed under a new imprint.
Further libel actions forced another hiatus in summer 1734. After briefly restarting in early 1735, the Register ceased later that year with issue 154, the title having “served its turn … to awaken the publick attention.”
Reception and influence
Contemporaries dubbed the sheet “Ralph’s Register.”
Its satirical essays and parliamentary reportage anticipated Ralph’s later work on The Champion, and Bob Harris ranks it among the “first sustained Patriot weeklies” of the 1730s.
